::: {.kw-overview}
This issue focuses predominantly on strategies to reduce ischaemic injury in deceased-donor kidneys. Two cohort studies evaluated normothermic techniques in donation after circulatory death (DCD). In donors aged 50 years or older, abdominal normothermic regional perfusion and ex situ normothermic machine perfusion were associated with comparable rates of delayed graft function, affecting approximately half of recipients. A single-region US series reported lower odds of delayed graft function with normothermic regional perfusion than with super-rapid recovery, despite an older donor population. A paired-donor study from India examined the retrieval sequence itself: removing one kidney before aortic cross-clamping reduced cold ischaemia time from approximately five hours to just over one hour. On donor utilisation, a meta-analysis of 457 recipients found that the risk of transmitting a multidrug-resistant Gram-negative organism was determined by the anatomical relationship between the site of colonisation and the graft, rather than by the resistance profile. In perioperative care, a randomised trial showed that Ringer's lactate preserved serum bicarbonate more effectively than a chloride-reduced saline–dextrose regimen and was associated with a higher eGFR at one month. The remaining studies address access to transplantation and rejection. A registry analysis of more than 180,000 transplants demonstrated a graded association between recipient obesity and delayed graft function; New Zealand data showed that candidates with a cPRA of 99% or above were transplanted at one-tenth the rate of those below 80%; and a Medicare claims study of almost 93,000 recipients ranked rejection phenotypes by their impact on graft survival.
:::

### 1. [Abdominal Normothermic Regional Perfusion Versus Normothermic Machine Perfusion of DCD Kidneys Aged 50 Years or Older: A Propensity Score Matched Analysis](https://doi.org/10.1111/aor.70234)
[Slagter JS, van de Geijn EF, de Goeij FHC, Groen PC, Schurink IJ, Alwyn IPJ, Porte RJ, Huurman VAL, de Jonge J, Minnee RC. *Artif Organs*, 2026. PMID: 42864868.]{.kw-ref}

Kidneys from older donors after circulatory death are used less frequently owing to their greater susceptibility to ischaemia–reperfusion injury, and the authors note that oxygenated hypothermic machine perfusion offers only partial mitigation. This study compared the two normothermic strategies now proposed for this role. Kidneys from donors aged 50 years or older that underwent abdominal normothermic regional perfusion (85 kidneys, from a national registry) were compared with kidneys that underwent ex situ normothermic machine perfusion (29 kidneys, from two clinical trials) using propensity score matching. The incidence of delayed graft function, the primary outcome, was high and similar in both groups (46% after regional perfusion and 52% after machine perfusion; p = 0.82). Rates of primary non-function (8% versus 7%) and acute rejection (25% versus 31%) did not differ, and death-censored graft survival and patient survival were comparable. Median eGFR at three years was 38 mL/min/1.73 m² in the regional perfusion group and 33 mL/min/1.73 m² in the machine perfusion group. The authors acknowledge that the study is non-randomised and small, and that the two arms were drawn from different data sources; the findings therefore establish the feasibility of both techniques rather than their equivalence. For UK centres evaluating normothermic strategies for older DCD kidneys, the study provides no clear basis for preferring either technique, and the choice is likely to be determined by logistics and local availability.

### 2. [Early Transplant Outcomes and Kidney Donor Profile Index Risk Prediction Performance in Kidneys Recovered Using a Uniform Abdominal Normothermic Regional Perfusion Technique](https://doi.org/10.1111/ctr.70729)
[Selim MA, Buff M, Fenlon M, Forbes A, Nwaduru C, Ovalle LA, Kohler R, Horns JJ, Botha J, Zimmerman MA. *Clin Transplant*, 2026. PMID: 42912555.]{.kw-ref}

The kidney donor profile index assigns a uniform risk weighting to all kidneys from donors after circulatory death and therefore cannot account for differences in recovery technique. This retrospective study from a single US donation service area included all kidney transplants from donors procured between January 2023 and December 2024. Of 523 transplants, 310 were from donors after brain death, 122 from DCD donors recovered by super-rapid recovery, and 91 from DCD donors recovered using a single standardised abdominal normothermic regional perfusion technique. Regional perfusion donors were older (median age 55 years, compared with 43.5 years for super-rapid recovery and 38 years for donors after brain death) and had higher donor profile index scores (66%, 53% and 27%, respectively). In multivariable models restricted to DCD donors, regional perfusion was associated with lower odds of delayed graft function than super-rapid recovery (odds ratio 0.445, 95% confidence interval 0.23 to 0.861), and each one-point increase in donor profile index was associated with higher odds of delayed graft function (odds ratio 1.028). One-year overall graft survival did not differ by recovery method. Interaction modelling suggested lower odds of delayed graft function for regional perfusion kidneys than for super-rapid recovery kidneys at equivalent index values, but the interaction term did not reach statistical significance; the study therefore cannot demonstrate that the index performs differently after regional perfusion. Follow-up was limited to one year. In the UK, where risk scoring of DCD offers likewise does not account for recovery technique, these findings suggest that kidneys recovered with regional perfusion may carry less early risk than the donor score implies, and they support the national collection of technique-specific outcome data.

### 3. [Sequential Kidney-First Retrieval and Early Graft Outcomes in Deceased Donor Kidney Transplantation: A Paired-Donor Comparative Cohort Study](https://doi.org/10.6002/ect.2026.0219)
[Kolte S, Kashiv P, Kriplani A, Munjewar C, Bhawane A, Khetan P, Khandekar AK, Deshpande N, Pasari A, Balwani M. *Exp Clin Transplant*, 2026. PMID: 42885705.]{.kw-ref}

In standard multiorgan retrieval the kidneys are removed last, which prolongs cold ischaemia time. This retrospective study from collaborating centres in central India evaluated an alternative sequence in 44 donors after brain death transplanted between January 2018 and December 2024. One kidney from each donor was removed before aortic cross-clamping, while the heart was still beating; the contralateral kidney was removed conventionally, after the thoracic and other abdominal organs. As each donor contributed one kidney to each arm, the 88 recipients constitute a paired comparison that controls for donor quality. Kidney-first retrieval substantially reduced cold ischaemia time (mean 78 versus 299 minutes). First-hour urine output was approximately twice as high (374 versus 186 mL), mean day-8 serum creatinine was 1.3 versus 3.1 mg/dL, and delayed graft function requiring dialysis decreased from 36.4% to 9.1% (p = 0.002). The combined incidence of retrieval injuries and post-transplant complications fell from 38.6% to 6.8%. Benefits of similar magnitude were observed for kidneys from expanded-criteria donors. On multivariable analysis, conventional (last) kidney removal was an independent predictor of delayed graft function (adjusted odds ratio 3.92, 95% confidence interval 1.41 to 10.87). The authors report that procurement of the other organs was not compromised; however, the abstract provides no thoracic or liver outcome data, the design is retrospective, and cold ischaemia times in both arms were short by most standards, which may limit generalisability to other systems. For UK multiorgan retrieval teams, the study primarily invites reconsideration of retrieval sequence and the transition from warm to cold ischaemia. Because the technique would alter the practice of thoracic and liver teams, prospective evidence, including outcomes for the other organs, would be required before adoption.

### 4. [Risk of Donor-Derived Infections From Organ Donors Colonized or Infected With Multidrug-Resistant Gram-Negative Bacteria: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis](https://doi.org/10.1111/ctr.70714)
[Paraskevas T, Chatzigrigoriadis C, Kostakis ID, Karydis N, Papasotiriou M, Ntrinias T, Maroulis I, Marangos M, Papachristou E, Grossi PA, Assimakopoulos SF. *Clin Transplant*, 2026. PMID: 42873093.]{.kw-ref}

Multidrug-resistant Gram-negative organisms are increasingly identified in potential donors, and national guidance on the use of such organs varies: Spanish and Scandinavian guidelines are more restrictive than the positions of the American and European societies. This review searched PubMed and Scopus for observational studies published between 2010 and 2025 and identified 12 cohort studies comprising 457 solid organ recipients, of whom 178 were kidney recipients. All studies involved deceased donors, and several were Chinese kidney series reporting carbapenem-resistant *Klebsiella* in preservation fluid. Overall, 29% of exposed recipients developed a donor-derived infection (95% confidence interval 11% to 49%; I² = 91.7%). Stratification by type of exposure revealed a clear gradient. In high-risk scenarios (donor bacteraemia, a positive preservation fluid culture, or a positive culture from the organ itself) the transmission rate was 40%, whereas when the organism was isolated only from a site unrelated to the graft the rate was effectively zero (0%, 95% confidence interval 0% to 1%; 128 recipients). A positive preservation fluid culture conferred the highest risk (58%, compared with 19% for donor bacteraemia). The pooled estimate for kidney transplants was 23%. Ninety-day mortality was 49% among recipients with a confirmed donor-derived infection and 6% among exposed recipients without infection. The review is limited by its reliance on aggregate data, small single-centre studies and inconsistent reporting of antimicrobial treatment. For UK kidney teams, the principal implication is that colonisation of a donor with a resistant organism at a site unrelated to the kidney should not in itself justify declining the organ, whereas a positive preservation fluid or urine culture warrants prompt communication between centres and targeted treatment of the recipient.

### 5. [Randomized Clinical Trial of Ringer's Lactate Versus Chloride-Reduced Saline-Dextrose in Postoperative Kidney Transplantation](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.ekir.2026.107081)
[Sawasdichai K, Rakpithayanon C, Konwai S, Wuttiputhanun T, Lumlertgul N, Apisutimaitri K, Burimsittichai R, Vorasittha A, Pobpan P, Tasanarong A, Leelahavanichkul A, Townamchai N, Praditpornsilpa K, Eiam-Ong S, Avihingsanon Y, Udomkarnjananun S. *Kidney Int Rep*, 2026. PMID: 42898223.]{.kw-ref}

Many fluid trials in transplantation have compared a balanced crystalloid with normal saline, a comparison likely to favour the balanced solution. This open-label trial at a single centre in Bangkok used a more rigorous comparator. Adult recipients of a first transplant were randomised, with stratification by donor type, to postoperative Ringer's lactate or to a dual infusion of normal saline and 5% dextrose designed to limit chloride load. Both regimens were titrated 1:1 to hourly urine output. Between September 2024 and March 2026, 159 patients were randomised; the prespecified modified intention-to-treat analysis included the 134 patients who received at least 2 litres of study fluid (67 per arm; 68.7% deceased-donor recipients). Total fluid volumes were similar (approximately 9.5 to 9.9 litres). On day 4, mean serum bicarbonate was 19.39 mEq/L with Ringer's lactate and 17.31 mEq/L with saline–dextrose (p < 0.001), and venous pH was 7.41 and 7.37, respectively. Rescue bicarbonate was required in 17.9% and 58.2% of patients. Mean eGFR at one month was 61.63 versus 53.18 mL/min/1.73 m² (p = 0.028). Delayed graft function occurred in 3.0% versus 9.0% (not statistically significant), and the full text indicates that most of the differences in graft function and biomarkers were confined to deceased-donor recipients. Hyperkalaemia and hyperglycaemia were infrequent in both arms. The trial was single-centre and open-label. It excluded the 25 recipients who were oligo-anuric from the outset and therefore provides limited information on those at greatest risk of delayed graft function; serum lactate was not routinely measured. For UK units, the trial supports the use of a single balanced crystalloid after transplantation, with Ringer's lactate as an inexpensive option, and the low and comparable rates of hyperkalaemia in both arms are relevant to units that continue to avoid potassium-containing fluids.

### 6. [Beyond Body Mass Index Cutoffs: Donor Quality and Ischemic Burden Shape Kidney Transplant Outcomes in Recipients With Severe Obesity: An Analysis of the Scientific Registry of Transplant Recipients Dataset](https://doi.org/10.6002/ect.2026.0093)
[Sharma R, Dwivedi AK. *Exp Clin Transplant*, 2026. PMID: 42885701.]{.kw-ref}

Body mass index thresholds continue to be used to restrict access to the transplant waiting list, although the evidence supporting specific cut-offs is limited. This analysis used aggregate summary tables from the Scientific Registry of Transplant Recipients for US deceased-donor kidney transplants performed between 2014 and 2024. Recipients were categorised by body mass index as below 35, 35 to 40, and above 40. Among 180,849 transplants (131,379 from donors after brain death and 49,470 from donors after circulatory death), the incidence of delayed graft function increased across categories (29.3%, 37.8% and 42.4%; p < 0.001). Relative to a body mass index below 35, the odds ratio for delayed graft function was 1.46 (95% confidence interval 1.42 to 1.51) for 35 to 40 and 1.77 (1.65 to 1.90) for above 40. For kidneys from donors after brain death, five-year graft survival declined from 77.51% to 74.33% and 70.03% across the three categories. The disadvantage associated with higher body mass index was evident at every level of donor profile index, donor age and cold ischaemia time, and the authors consider it greatest when obesity coincided with less favourable donor or ischaemic characteristics. Because the analysis relies on aggregate tables with Kaplan–Meier estimates and unadjusted comparisons rather than patient-level multivariable models, confounding by recipient factors associated with obesity cannot be excluded. Nor does it compare transplanted obese patients with comparable patients who remained on dialysis, which is the comparison that determines whether listing is beneficial. For UK units making listing decisions, the study supports matching recipients with severe obesity to lower-risk kidneys with short cold ischaemia times, rather than excluding them on the basis of body mass index alone.

### 7. [Rates of Deceased Donor Kidney Transplantation in Highly Sensitised Patients in Aotearoa New Zealand: A Data Linkage Analysis](https://doi.org/10.1111/nep.70295)
[Thomas AOR, Hedley JA, Shettigar R, Cross NB, Dittmer I, Dunckley H, Webster AC. *Nephrology (Carlton)*, 2026. PMID: 42878695.]{.kw-ref}

This study was designed to inform potential revisions to the national kidney allocation scheme in Aotearoa New Zealand by examining outcomes for highly sensitised candidates under the existing scheme. The authors used linked health data from the AcceSS and Equity in Transplantation platform to identify all patients listed for a deceased-donor kidney between 2006 and 2019. Patients with a panel reactive antibody or calculated panel reactive antibody of 80% or higher were classified as highly sensitised and subdivided into 80–94%, 95–98% and 99% or above. Previous transplantation, female sex, younger age and non-European ethnicity were each associated with greater sensitisation (all p < 0.001). The rate of transplantation declined with increasing sensitisation. Compared with candidates below 80%, the hazard ratio for transplantation was 0.75 at 80–94% (95% confidence interval 0.54 to 1.04; not significant), 0.38 at 95–98% (0.23 to 0.60) and 0.10 at 99% or above (0.05 to 0.17). The abstract does not report absolute numbers in each category, waiting times, or the extent to which living donation or desensitisation offset the disparity. As the study period ends in 2019, it also predates any recent changes to allocation. The authors identify the group at 99% or above as the clear priority for reform. For UK clinicians reviewing the treatment of sensitised patients within allocation schemes, these data indicate that the substantial disadvantage is concentrated at the extreme upper end of the range, which supports allocation priority targeted at candidates with a cPRA of 99% or more rather than extended to all those above 80%.

### 8. [Claims-Based Phenotyping of Acute Kidney Transplant Rejection in a National Medicare Cohort](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.ekir.2026.107060)
[Ekanayake C, Yu M, Natarajan K, Husain SA, Muppavarapu CS, Schold J, Mohan S. *Kidney Int Rep*, 2026. PMID: 42898365.]{.kw-ref}

Transplant registries generally record acute rejection as a binary variable, which provides no information on how outcomes vary by rejection type. This study used US Renal Data System claims for 92,845 adult recipients of a first kidney-only transplant performed between 2012 and 2021 with Medicare as the primary payer. Rejection within the first year was identified from transplant-complication codes combined with antirejection treatment within 14 days, and the treatment modality was used to infer the phenotype: intravenous corticosteroids alone for mild cellular rejection, thymoglobulin for severe cellular rejection, plasmapheresis with or without immunoglobulin for antibody-mediated rejection, and combined therapy for mixed rejection. Of 5,712 episodes, 69.4% were classified as mild cellular, 8.8% as severe cellular, 19.7% as antibody-mediated and 2.1% as mixed. Among the 3,052 episodes preceded by a biopsy, three-year death-censored graft survival was 87.9% for mild cellular, 80.7% for severe cellular, 73.5% for antibody-mediated and 68.4% for mixed rejection. In adjusted time-varying Cox models, the corresponding hazard ratios for graft failure relative to recipients without rejection were 1.84, 2.50, 4.18 and 4.59. In the absence of a preceding biopsy the gradient was less consistent, and severe cellular rejection carried no excess risk after adjustment, suggesting misclassification when histology was unavailable. The algorithm was not validated against pathology reports, and privately insured recipients were excluded. For UK practice, the magnitude of the excess risk associated with antibody-mediated and mixed rejection supports early biopsy and intensive follow-up after such episodes, and the study illustrates the additional value that national registries would offer if they recorded rejection type and treatment.
